purpose: Editorial evidence for replacing specimen-checklist prose with chronological model development. Do not publish these source links; retain internally.
method: Read current guide and prior article evidence, then fetched the listed sources. Dates below distinguish factory/catalog events from individual examples. No exact cutoff inferred from one guitar.

12-string.recommendedFocus: The D12-20 and D12-35 regular-production sequence, followed by pickguard and bridge-plate changes. Earlier special orders belong in one short background paragraph, not the main changes table.

rows.change: First D12-20 instruments completed; Martin establishes a regular-production twelve-string dreadnought.
D12-20 enters the catalog with mahogany back and sides, spruce top, rosewood fingerboard and bridge, a slotted headstock and a 12-fret body joint.
D12-35 joins the line with a three-piece Brazilian rosewood back, bound ebony fingerboard and ebony bridge. Both original D12 models use a 24.9-inch scale and 1 7/8-inch nut.
rows.scope: D12-35 introduction and initial model distinction
rows.status: supported by introductory history plus firsthand original specimens

rows.change: Black pickguards replace the earlier tortoise-pattern material during the production transition.
rows.scope: Both D12 models; avoid claiming January 1 or every 1967 instrument
rows.caveat: A currently indexed Folkway 1967 D12-20 still has a tortoise-pattern guard, so use transition wording: https://folkwaymusic.com/product/?prod_id=35402%2F

rows.change: Rosewood bridge plates replace the earlier maple construction as Martin strengthens its dreadnought design.
rows.scope: D12-20 explicitly corroborated; Martin company history gives the broader April 9, 1968 change
rows.status: supported for material change; do not attach a precise D12 serial cutoff or plate dimension

rows.change: The D12-35 reaches Martin's transition from Brazilian to East Indian rosewood for standard rosewood bodies.
rows.scope: Company-wide material transition relevant to D12-35; no D12-specific first serial found
rows.caveat: Do not say every 1969 D12-35 is Brazilian or assign D-21 serial 254498 to a D12-35.

background.fact: A purpose-built twelve-string 00-21 was shipped in 1921; the 1932 C-2 order shows later archtop experimentation. These were special orders, not a continuous catalog D12 line.
background.limit: Avoid prewar total: Corwin's archtop and twelve-string pages disagree. Avoid calling the 1932 February 18 date both stamping and shipping.

omitOrQualify: Do not carry the Twelfth Fret repaired 1968 guitar's oversized maple replacement plate or concealed bolts into factory specifications.
Do not date D12-20 rosewood fingerboard/headplate species to a universal 1967 cutoff from the Twelfth Fret example.
No verified factory tuner-switch date or D12-specific reinforcement cutoff was found; do not import a general six-string rule.
Do not add D12-45 to the regular line solely from a reported 1969 special order.

tenor.recommendedFocus: Body redesign and model succession: size 5 beginnings, the 14-fret experiments, shortened size 0 body, belly bridge, then the simpler mahogany postwar models.

rows.change: Martin introduces its tenor family in size 5, including the mahogany 5-17T and spruce/rosewood 5-21T.
The 2-18TL experiments with a 14-fret neck on the earlier body outline, placing the bridge higher on the top.
rows.scope: Design experiment; not all tenor models changed in 1928

rows.change: The Carl Fischer tenor shortens the upper body to accommodate 14 clear frets with improved bridge placement.
rows.scope: Carl Fischer design, ancestor of the regular 0-18T

rows.change: The design enters the regular Martin line as the 0-18T, whose upper bout becomes wider and flatter.
rows.status: supported; model already appears in 1929 records, so do not call 1930 its first ever production

rows.change: The 0-18T's straight bridge gives way to the belly bridge.
The 0-17T adds an all-mahogany alternative in the larger tenor body.
rows.status: supported by production table and independent tenor reference

rows.change: The 5-15T replaces the 5-17T, retaining the small mahogany body but using the simpler finish associated with Style 15.
rows.status: corroborated by two dealers with firsthand instruments; not a factory ledger citation

rows.change: The 0-15T offers the larger mahogany tenor in plain Style 15 appointments and satin finish.
rows.status: supported by model chronology and firsthand 1960/1962 examples

omitOrQualify: 0-17T last-production year varies between sources (1960 versus 1963); do not create a definitive discontinuation row without factory records.
Do not make a generic six-string 1934 12-to-14-fret transition the tenor transition; these models followed their own earlier sequence.
Do not call every size 5 tenor a 23-inch scale: 5-21T and 5-15T examples differ.
StewMac's Dick Boak video has an on-screen '1927 5-15T' label conflicting with other sources; do not import that model/date combination.
Banjo-style tuners and early decal dates are not exact family-wide switches established by this research.

plectrum.recommendedFocus: Short-lived growth from small size-1 bodies to 000 and OM bodies; distinguish production ending from old inventory remaining on sale.

rows.change: Early plectrums use size-1 bodies, with a long four-string neck intended for plectrum-banjo players.
Martin expands into the larger 000-18P and the 14-fret OM-18P.
rows.scope: New body formats alongside size-1 models

rows.change: OM-18P production reaches 65 instruments for the year; small numbers of C-1 and C-2 archtop plectrums are also made.
rows.scope: Annual production and new archtop branch
rows.status: supported; 65 is not lifetime OM-18P production

rows.change: Regular plectrum production ends.
rows.scope: Regular production, not every future special order or catalog appearance

rows.change: OM-18P remains offered for sale after the main production period.
rows.scope: Sales availability, not newly built guitars
rows.caveat: Do not repeat Gruhn's conflicting assertion that all examples were built in 1931; Corwin documents a stamped 1930 instrument and 30 built that year.

rows.change: Isolated plectrum orders follow the discontinued regular line: two in 1940 and one in 1941.

stableDesignFacts.fact: The plectrum format pairs a longer scale with four strings; the OM-18P uses the 15-inch body, spruce top, mahogany back and sides, and ebony fittings of its OM family.

omitOrQualify: Corwin introductory prose says plectrums appeared in 1930 but his production table begins 1928; use the model-specific table, not that broad sentence.
Do not turn 1930 OM-18P teardrop guards or banjo tuners into a later universal transition without dated production evidence.
Do not use inconsistent 1-28P scale measurements from Wildwood as a factory specification.
A six-string conversion is later work, not a historical factory model change.

archtop.recommendedFocus: The C, R and F families evolve in parallel. Track soundholes, pressed-versus-carved tops, body size and model additions separately.

rows.change: The C-series launches with 15-inch bodies, carved spruce tops and round soundholes; C-1 uses mahogany, while C-2 and C-3 use rosewood with progressively fancier trim.
F-holes replace the early round-hole C design. The smaller R-18 begins with a pressed spruce top and also moves from round soundhole to f-holes during this period.
rows.scope: Transition window; different schedules by model
rows.caveat: Do not say all C models changed in 1933 or use Corwin's internally conflicting claim that the September 1933 R-18 was Martin's first f-hole guitar.

rows.change: The R-17 adds a mahogany-topped version to the smaller archtop family.
The F-7 and F-9 expand the archtop body to 16 inches and introduce a more elaborate upper tier.
R-18 changes from a pressed top with segmented f-holes to a carved top with continuous f-holes.
The F-1 and F-2 join the 16-inch family with simpler appointments; F-1 has mahogany back and sides, F-2 rosewood.
Acoustic archtop production closes: final C guitars in August, final F batch in September and final R-18 batch in November.
rows.scope: End of original acoustic archtop line
rows.status: supported by Corwin's documented final-batch examples

supportingFact.fact: 401 F-series acoustic archtops were made, including 91 F-1s.

omitOrQualify: Exact C-series scale-change year conflicts: Folkway gives 1933; Corwin gives 1934 and measures the nominal scales differently. Omit an exact scale-year row; describe early long-scale versus later short-scale only if needed.
The later electric F-series is unrelated to the 1930s acoustic F-series despite the letter.
Do not claim all archtops have carved backs; Martin shaped thin back plates with braces.
Do not import F-5 production details without another verified source.

electric.recommendedFocus: Three successive designs: electrified acoustic flat-tops, thin hollowbody F-series and redesigned GT-series.

rows.change: The 00-18E joins Martin's electrified flat-tops with a DeArmond pickup and top-mounted volume and tone controls; a second pickup was available.
rows.scope: 00-18E; dedicated existing JVG page covers D-18E/D-28E

rows.change: F-50, F-55 and F-65 prototypes launch a thin hollowbody electric design. F-50 has one pickup; F-55 adds two pickups; F-65 adds a second cutaway.
rows.scope: F-series prototypes and first small batches

rows.change: The F-series moves into larger production, using an adjustable clear plexiglass bridge.
00-18E production ends; remaining stock is still listed in the following year's price list.
rows.scope: Production distinct from continued sales listing

rows.change: F-series production ends as the GT-70 and GT-75 arrive. The GT-70 is single-cutaway; GT-75 is double-cutaway. Both offer an optional Bigsby vibrato and an adjustable neck rod.
GT-70 production ends, leaving the GT-75 to continue into 1967.
A GT-75 twelve-string version appears briefly with an elongated conventional headstock. GT-series production ends that year.
rows.status: supported by collector's documented instruments and original marketing material

rows.change: GT models still appear in catalogs and price lists after production has stopped.
rows.scope: Availability, not an additional manufacturing year

supportingFact.fact: F-50 production totaled 519, with only one made in its final year, 1965.

omitOrQualify: Do not give an F-55 total; Corwin's page has conflicting labels/counts.
Do not give an exact burgundy-to-red cutoff: Marshall explicitly describes the early-1966 change as undocumented and approximate.
Do not assign every headstock outline to one exact year; Marshall documents variants and exceptions.
Do not say only three GT-75-12 guitars existed; Marshall disputes that count.
Do not confuse catalog listings in 1968 with guitars built in 1968.

writingRecommendation: Use a two-column Year / What Changed table, followed by short era sections explaining the physical difference. Remove photograph requests, seller troubleshooting, conversion warnings and a stack of specimen dates from the main narrative. Retain one concise identification section and relevant internal links. When evidence does not support a model-specific cutoff, omit the cutoff rather than disguising a specimen as a factory change.
